Chapter 7: The Limits of Human Understanding—Error, Will, and Judgment
Even if you've got a solid method for thinking things through, your mind still isn't immune to making mistakes. Why do errors creep in, even when we're careful? Understanding that "why" is key—not just for staying humble, but for sharpening the way you search for truth.
Let’s picture your mind as having two main parts: the understanding, and the will. The understanding—or your intellect—is kind of like a lantern. It lights up just a small patch at a time, showing you what’s right in front of you. The will, though, is more like a pair of wings. It can take off and soar way beyond what the lantern actually reveals.
And here’s where things get tricky. Problems start when your will jumps ahead—making choices or judgments about things your understanding hasn’t clearly seen. It’s a bit like trying to leap across a canyon without first checking if there’s solid ground on the other side. When your will goes beyond the light of your understanding, mistakes are almost inevitable.
So, how can you keep your mind on the right track? There are a few simple habits that really help:
First, try to suspend judgment when things aren’t clear. If you don’t have a clear and distinct understanding, it’s actually smarter to wait before deciding—rather than risk being wrong.
Second, practice patience and humility. Remind yourself that your understanding has its limits, and rushing to conclusions can easily backfire.
Third, make it a habit to review your decisions regularly. Think of it like a gardener checking for weeds—when you revisit your judgments, you catch mistakes early, before they spread.
When you put these guidelines into practice, your will and your understanding start working in harmony. You let your choices be guided by what you really know—so errors become fewer, and when they do happen, they're not as serious.
Here’s a real-world example. Imagine you’re learning a new language. It’s so tempting to just guess what unfamiliar words mean. But if you keep guessing without checking, you’ll end up with a pile of misunderstandings. When you pause to verify those meanings—maybe by looking them up—you avoid building your knowledge on shaky ground.
Now, realizing that your understanding has limits? That’s not something to feel bad about. In fact, it’s a call to be more careful and more self-aware.
The more you respect those limits, the more skillful and honest your thinking becomes—and the closer you get to real, lasting truth.
